title: Review—Measurement and Analysis of Cancer Biomarkers Based on Electrochemical Biosensors

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Molecular Landscape of Cancer Biomarkers
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical and Molecular Landscape of Cancer Biomarkers - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Cancer biomarkers comprise a heterogeneous set of measurable molecules that reflect tumor initiation, progression, and response to therapy. In the context of electrochemical biosensing, the most practically important classes include circulating proteins and glycoproteins, tumor-associated antibodies, nucleic-acid targets, and cell-derived components released into accessible biofluids. Protein biomarkers remain central to clinical translation because they are directly linked to disease phenotype and are often present in serum, plasma, or whole blood, making them compatible with minimally invasive testing workflows ref [16], ref [22].

The clinical value of these biomarkers depends not only on biological relevance but also on their abundance range, matrix complexity, and molecular recognition requirements. Many cancer-associated proteins occur at low concentrations in early-stage disease and must be distinguished from structurally similar background species in complex samples, which places strict demands on affinity, specificity, and non-specific adsorption control. Antibody-based capture remains a dominant strategy for addressing these requirements, while engineered antibody derivatives offer opportunities to improve stability, orientation, and assay performance in biosensor formats ref [32], ref [22].

From an analytical perspective, the cancer biomarker landscape is therefore inseparable from figures of merit such as sensitivity, limit of detection, selectivity, dynamic range, reproducibility, and clinical robustness. These parameters determine whether a biomarker assay is useful for screening, prognosis, treatment monitoring, or recurrence surveillance. Recent biosensor research increasingly couples nanostructured interfaces and simplified assay architectures, including no-wash formats, to improve performance in clinically relevant matrices and shorten turnaround time, which is particularly important for point-of-care oncology diagnostics ref [37], ref [43], ref [16].

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Molecular Landscape of Cancer Biomarkers
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical and Molecular Landscape of Cancer Biomarkers - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
An important dimension of the clinical biomarker landscape is the shift from single soluble proteins toward multiplexed and non-invasive analytes that better reflect tumor heterogeneity. Beyond conventional serum markers, clinically relevant cancer information is increasingly obtained from circulating exosomes, hormone dysregulation, and treatment-related molecules measured in blood, urine, saliva, or other accessible specimens. This expansion is especially significant for early detection and longitudinal monitoring, where repeated sampling must be minimally invasive, analytically robust, and compatible with low-abundance targets ref [9], ref [29], ref [35].

Exosomes have emerged as particularly informative biomarkers because they encapsulate tumor-derived proteins, nucleic acids, and lipids within stable vesicles, thereby preserving molecular signatures of the originating cancer cells. Their presence in peripheral biofluids makes them attractive for liquid biopsy applications, but their small size, compositional complexity, and low concentration impose stringent analytical demands on capture efficiency and signal amplification. Reviews of exosome-focused biosensing therefore emphasize the need for platforms capable of selective isolation and sensitive electrochemical readout in complex clinical matrices ref [9], ref [35].

Hormonal biomarkers represent another clinically important class, especially in hormone-dependent malignancies such as breast and prostate cancer, where endocrine status can inform diagnosis, stratification, and therapy response. Likewise, monitoring antineoplastic drugs and related treatment molecules can provide indirect but clinically actionable information on therapeutic exposure, resistance, and toxicity. Electrochemical approaches are well suited to these applications because they can be adapted to small molecules as well as vesicular targets, and carbon nanomaterial-enabled transducers are particularly promising for non-invasive sampling and early-stage screening, including breast cancer-oriented assays ref [32], ref [34], ref [29], ref [38].

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Molecular Landscape of Cancer Biomarkers
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical and Molecular Landscape of Cancer Biomarkers - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
At the molecular level, nucleic-acid biomarkers occupy a central position in cancer diagnostics because they report directly on dysregulated gene expression and tumor-associated sequence signatures. Among these, microRNAs (miRNAs) are especially important owing to their aberrant expression across many malignancies, their regulatory roles in proliferation, invasion, apoptosis, and metastasis, and their presence in accessible biofluids. Their short length, low abundance, and high sequence homology, however, impose stringent analytical requirements on biosensor design, particularly in terms of selectivity for single-base discrimination and sensitivity at very low concentrations ref [6], ref [31].

These properties make nucleic-acid biomarkers highly relevant for early detection, disease stratification, and longitudinal monitoring, but they also explain why label-free and amplification-integrated transduction strategies have become prominent. Label-free biosensors are attractive in this setting because they can simplify workflows, reduce assay time, and preserve target integrity, which is advantageous for clinical testing of fragile RNA species ref [14]. More broadly, DNA- and enzyme-based biosensing architectures have provided the conceptual and analytical foundation for recognizing short oligonucleotides with improved signal conversion, hybridization efficiency, and multiplexing potential, all of which are desirable for profiling tumor-associated miRNA panels rather than relying on a single marker ref [16].

Although developed in different disease contexts, broader biosensor reviews also underscore a general principle relevant to oncology: clinically useful molecular biomarkers require not only biological specificity but also compatibility with minimally invasive sampling and scalable detection platforms ref [23]. This is reflected in emerging cancer-oriented implementations such as microfluidic paper-based electrochemical/visual systems for miR-21, a widely studied oncomiR, which illustrate how portable platforms may support decentralized screening and recurrence surveillance when analytical sensitivity and operational simplicity are jointly optimized ref [31].

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Molecular Landscape of Cancer Biomarkers
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical and Molecular Landscape of Cancer Biomarkers - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A clinically important dimension of the cancer biomarker landscape is the coexistence of circulating proteins, intracellular tumor-suppressor products, viral oncogene nucleic acids, and metabolically related peptide signals, each of which reflects a different layer of tumor biology. Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) remains a prototypical serum protein marker for screening and disease monitoring in prostate cancer, whereas p53 is more closely linked to genomic instability and malignant transformation. At the nucleic-acid level, oncogenic viral sequences such as human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA are highly relevant in cervical and other HPV-associated cancers, illustrating how biomarker classes span host-derived and pathogen-derived targets ref [20], ref [13], ref [23], ref [40].

This molecular heterogeneity has direct analytical implications for electrochemical biosensing. Protein biomarkers often require highly selective immunointerfaces and broad dynamic range in complex biofluids, as illustrated by electrochemical immunosensors for PSA and p53 ref [20], ref [13]. By contrast, DNA biomarkers demand sequence-specific hybridization with stringent mismatch discrimination, a challenge emphasized in electrochemical DNA sensing strategies for cancer-related nucleic acids and HPV oncogene detection ref [23], ref [40]. Label-free impedimetric and redox-capacitive transduction are especially attractive in this context because they can monitor interfacial binding events without extensive labeling chemistry, supporting simplified assay architectures for clinically relevant targets ref [35].

From a translational perspective, the diversity of cancer biomarkers also motivates adaptable sensing materials and device formats. Nanoporous anodic alumina platforms offer tunable architectures for biomarker capture and signal generation across clinically significant analytes ref [20], while nanostructured electrode modifiers such as nickel nanoparticles have demonstrated the broader feasibility of ultrasensitive peptide and hormone detection in electrochemical formats ref [21]. Collectively, these studies underscore that clinically useful cancer biosensors must be tailored not only to sensitivity requirements, but also to the molecular origin, abundance range, and sample-matrix context of each biomarker class ref [20], ref [21], ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Molecular Landscape of Cancer Biomarkers
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical and Molecular Landscape of Cancer Biomarkers - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A clinically important dimension of the cancer biomarker landscape is the transition from tissue-confined markers to circulating molecular signatures that better support longitudinal monitoring. In this context, nucleic acids and exosome-associated cargo are especially valuable because they can reflect tumor genotype, transcriptional state, and intercellular signaling in minimally invasive samples. Reviews of nucleic-acid and exosome biosensing emphasize that these analytes expand the biomarker concept beyond conventional proteins, enabling earlier detection, molecular stratification, and dynamic assessment of treatment response or relapse through liquid biopsy-type workflows ref [25].

Among nucleic-acid biomarkers, tumor-related DNA sequences remain central because they provide direct evidence of oncogenic alteration and can be targeted with high sequence specificity. Electrochemical DNA biosensors developed for breast-cancer gene markers illustrate how clinically relevant mutations or gene fragments can be detected in a label-free format, supporting the broader role of genomic biomarkers in precision oncology ref [13]. More generally, analyses of electrochemical DNA biosensor performance show a sustained reduction in detection limits over time, underscoring the analytical push needed to measure scarce circulating tumor DNA and other low-abundance cancer-associated sequences in real samples ref [37]. Nanostructured DNA-sensing interfaces further highlight that cancer-cell DNA can also be interrogated to study drug–DNA interactions, linking biomarker analysis with therapeutic evaluation ref [39].

The biomarker landscape also includes soluble signaling mediators and disease-specific panels that reflect tumor microenvironment activity and organ-specific pathology. For example, chemokine ligands measured in colorectal cancer models demonstrate the relevance of inflammatory and migratory signaling molecules as complementary biomarkers to nucleic acids and canonical antigens ref [24]. In melanoma, current diagnostic analyses likewise rely on integrating multiple molecular and clinical indicators rather than a single marker, reinforcing the need for multiplexed and context-aware biosensing strategies ref [34]. Taken together, the diversity of biomarker classes imposes stringent analytical requirements on electrochemical platforms, including high sensitivity, selectivity in complex biofluids, and compatibility with serial monitoring across the cancer care continuum ref [25].

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Biosensing Principles and Signal Transduction Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Electrochemical Biosensing Principles and Signal Transduction Strategies - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Electrochemical biosensors for cancer biomarkers operate by coupling a selective biorecognition layer to an electrode interface that converts binding or hybridization events into electrical signals. In practice, the recognition element may be an antibody, nucleic acid probe, molecularly imprinted polymer, or related affinity structure, while the transducer measures changes in current, potential, conductance, or interfacial impedance produced by target capture ref [14], ref [21], ref [22], ref [32]. This architecture is attractive for oncology because it enables direct analysis of proteins, nucleic acids, and other clinically relevant analytes in miniaturizable and potentially low-cost formats ref [16], ref [37].

From a signal-transduction perspective, the main electrochemical modes include amperometric/voltammetric detection, potentiometric readout, and impedimetric or conductometric sensing. Amperometric and voltammetric schemes quantify faradaic currents arising from redox-active labels, mediators, or electrocatalytic amplification; potentiometric formats monitor equilibrium potential shifts; and impedance-based methods track changes in charge-transfer resistance, double-layer properties, or dielectric behavior after analyte binding ref [14], ref [22], ref [37]. For nucleic-acid targets, hybridization at electrode-confined probes can be translated into current or impedance changes, forming the basis of DNA electrochemical biosensing strategies highly relevant to mutation and oncogene analysis ref [38].

Signal quality is strongly governed by the physicochemical properties of the electrode surface. Nanomaterials and nanostructures are widely used to increase active area, accelerate electron transfer, improve probe loading, and support signal amplification, thereby enhancing sensitivity and lowering detection limits ref [31], ref [16]. In parallel, synthetic recognition layers such as molecularly imprinted polymers provide a route to robust, selective sensing when biological receptors are unstable or costly, broadening the design space for cancer biomarker assays ref [21]. Collectively, these principles define the foundation on which more specialized electrochemical sensing formats for cancer diagnostics are built.

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Biosensing Principles and Signal Transduction Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Electrochemical Biosensing Principles and Signal Transduction Strategies - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central signal-transduction route in electrochemical biosensors is amperometric and voltammetric readout, in which a biorecognition event modulates the faradaic current of an electroactive species. In enzyme-based architectures, target binding either generates or consumes redox-active products such as H2O2, allowing current to scale with analyte concentration; this principle is well established in oxidase-type biosensors and remains highly relevant for catalytic cancer biomarker assays ref [8], ref [37]. The use of electrocatalytic mediators further improves transduction efficiency by lowering overpotential and suppressing interference from complex biofluids ref [10].

Prussian Blue is a representative example of an electron-transfer mediator that has been widely exploited for sensitive H2O2 reduction, enabling low-potential amperometric detection in disposable sensor formats ref [10]. More broadly, nanomaterial-enabled electrodes based on carbon nanostructures, metal nanoparticles, and hybrid nanocomposites enhance active surface area, conductivity, and biomolecule loading, thereby amplifying current responses and accelerating interfacial charge transfer ref [29], ref [37]. These features are particularly useful for low-abundance cancer biomarkers, where small recognition-induced changes must be converted into robust analytical signals.

In practical cancer diagnostics, these transduction strategies have been adapted to diverse analyte classes, including proteins, hormones, and small signaling molecules. Electrochemical hormone biosensors illustrate how amperometric or voltammetric formats can quantify clinically relevant low-level targets through selective receptor or enzyme coupling ref [32], while broader biosensor classifications emphasize the importance of matching the transduction mode to the biochemical recognition mechanism and sample matrix ref [35]. Similar principles underpin early breast-cancer screening platforms, where electrochemical detection translates antigen–antibody or nucleic-acid hybridization events into measurable current changes with high analytical sensitivity ref [38]. Related small-molecule sensing concepts, such as catalytic electroanalysis of hydrogen sulfide, also demonstrate how analyte-specific redox chemistry can be harnessed as a direct electrical output in biomedical biosensing ref [41].

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Biosensing Principles and Signal Transduction Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Electrochemical Biosensing Principles and Signal Transduction Strategies - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central signal-transduction route in cancer electrochemical biosensing is label-free readout, in which target binding alters interfacial charge transfer, double-layer structure, or electrode capacitance without requiring enzymatic or nanoparticle tags. This strategy is attractive for clinical biomarker analysis because it simplifies assay architecture, reduces reagent consumption, and preserves native binding events, particularly for proteins and nucleic acids present at low abundance. Reviews of diagnostic label-free platforms emphasize that impedance-, capacitance-, and voltammetry-based schemes are especially suited to monitoring surface-confined recognition processes in real time or near real time ref [14], ref [16].

Within this framework, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy has become one of the most widely used methods for converting molecular recognition into measurable electrical outputs. Hybridization of cancer-associated microRNAs or binding of protein biomarkers typically increases steric hindrance and modifies electron-transfer resistance, whereas changes in probe density and interfacial organization can also affect capacitive responses. The utility of such mechanisms for nucleic-acid targets, including microRNAs relevant to oncology, is highlighted in dedicated reviews of electrochemical miRNA biosensors ref [16]. At the same time, rigorous interpretation of label-free signals requires attention to analytical figures of merit, especially uncertainty propagation and realistic determination of the limit of detection, since nonspecific adsorption and baseline drift can strongly influence low-signal measurements ref [7].

Recent device-level developments further show that signal-transduction strategy is inseparable from platform integration. Microfluidic electronic biosensors improve mass transport, support multiplexed biomarker panels, and enable smaller sample volumes, thereby enhancing the practical value of impedance and voltammetric transduction for cancer diagnostics ref [24]. Paper-based and hybrid electrochemical/visual systems illustrate how catalytic amplification can be coupled to nucleic-acid recognition when label-free sensitivity alone is insufficient; for example, miR-21 sensing on microfluidic paper platforms demonstrates how portable architectures can combine electrochemical quantification with user-friendly readout ref [31]. Together, these advances indicate that modern cancer biosensors increasingly balance the simplicity of label-free detection with selective amplification and integrated sample handling to achieve clinically meaningful performance ref [14], ref [24].

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Biosensing Principles and Signal Transduction Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Electrochemical Biosensing Principles and Signal Transduction Strategies - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A major signal-transduction route in cancer electrochemical biosensors is impedance- and capacitance-based readout, where biorecognition is translated into changes in interfacial charge-transfer resistance, double-layer capacitance, or dielectric properties at the electrode surface. In affinity architectures, binding of proteins or nucleic acids perturbs electron transfer of a redox probe or the intrinsic capacitive behavior of the interface, enabling label-free quantification with minimal assay complexity. These mechanisms are especially attractive for cancer biomarkers because they can capture surface-confined hybridization or antigen–antibody events without enzymatic labels while still offering high sensitivity to nanoscale interfacial rearrangements ref [35], ref [17].

For nucleic-acid biomarkers, impedimetric transduction is widely used to follow DNA hybridization through steric blocking and electrostatic repulsion effects after target capture. Studies comparing modified glassy carbon electrodes incorporating RGO and MWCNT-based nanomaterials show that electrode composition strongly governs hybridization-induced impedance shifts by altering probe loading, conductivity, and interfacial heterogeneity ref [24]. More broadly, DNA-based electrochemical strategies for cancer biomarker analysis exploit these same principles to detect mutation-related or expression-related sequences, with nanostructured transducers improving signal gain and lowering detection limits ref [40]. Graphene and related low-dimensional conductors further enhance this mode by providing high carrier mobility and large accessible surface area, thereby amplifying conductivity changes arising from biomolecular adsorption or hybridization events ref [17].

Although often discussed separately from amperometry, impedance and capacitive methods are frequently integrated with nanomaterial-assisted current transduction in practical immunosensors. Conductive nanocomposites such as chitosan/carbon black films or AuNPs@g-C3N4 hybrids increase the effective electrode area, facilitate antibody immobilization, and improve electron-transfer kinetics, so that target binding yields larger measurable perturbations in either faradaic current or interfacial resistance. Representative cancer biomarker platforms for p53 and prostate-specific antigen illustrate how nanostructured interfaces convert recognition into ultrasensitive electrical outputs while preserving assay specificity ref [13], ref [18]. From a design perspective, these trends parallel broader developments in nanomaterial-based amperometric biosensors, where the transducer is engineered to maximize coupling between molecular recognition and electrical signal generation ref [42].

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Biosensing Principles and Signal Transduction Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Electrochemical Biosensing Principles and Signal Transduction Strategies - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
An important signal-transduction theme in electrochemical cancer biosensing is label-free operation, where target binding directly perturbs interfacial charge transfer, capacitance, conductivity, or field-effect behavior without secondary tags. In nucleic-acid assays, hybridization at the electrode surface can be read from changes in intrinsic electrochemical response, as demonstrated in label-free DNA platforms for breast-cancer gene markers; more broadly, the steady improvement of detection limits in electrochemical DNA biosensors reflects progressive optimization of probe density, interface architecture, and low-noise readout rather than reliance solely on external labels ref [13], ref [37].

The efficiency of this transduction step is strongly governed by nanoscale interface design. Nitrogen-doped graphene quantum dots (N-GQDs) enhance electron-transfer kinetics, enlarge electroactive area, and provide abundant sites for biomolecule immobilization, thereby amplifying small recognition-induced electrical changes in voltammetric or impedimetric formats ref [22]. Likewise, aptamer-based label-free sensing highlights how receptor conformation and surface organization shape the electrical output: comparative lysozyme aptasensor studies show that different aptamer sequences can produce markedly different analytical responses even for the same target, underscoring that bioreceptor selection is itself a transduction variable ref [15].

A related design principle is control of the distance and orientation between the recognition layer and the electrode. In peptide-based electrochemical biosensors, spacer length modulates accessibility to proteases and the efficiency with which cleavage events are converted into current or impedance changes, illustrating how molecular-scale geometry dictates signal generation ref [32]. Field-effect transduction extends the same concept to semiconductor interfaces, where analyte-triggered local pH or charge variations are converted into gate-potential shifts, as shown in pH-sensitive FET biosensors coupled to enzymatic recognition ref [23]. For cancer biomarker analysis, these examples collectively show that sensitivity depends not only on affinity, but on how effectively molecular recognition is translated into an interfacial electrical perturbation measurable by the chosen electrochemical platform ref [13], ref [22], ref [23].

subsections.section_title: Biorecognition Elements and Interfacial Engineering for Cancer Biosensors
subsections.subsection_title: Biorecognition Elements and Interfacial Engineering for Cancer Biosensors - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A central design variable in electrochemical cancer biosensors is the choice of biorecognition element, because selectivity, assay format, and long-term stability are all rooted in the nature of the capture layer. Antibodies remain the dominant affinity probes for protein biomarkers owing to their high specificity and established coupling chemistries, which has made immunosensors a major platform for cancer-related analytes such as PSA, CEA, and HER2 ref [14], ref [32]. In parallel, nucleic-acid probes enable highly selective hybridization-based recognition of oncogenes, circulating tumor DNA, and microRNA targets, offering straightforward sequence programmability and compatibility with label-free electrochemical transduction ref [38], ref [16].

Interfacial engineering determines whether these recognition capabilities are translated into measurable analytical performance. Nanostructured electrode coatings increase electroactive surface area, improve electron-transfer kinetics, and provide higher loading of antibodies or DNA probes, but they must also preserve biomolecular activity and suppress nonspecific adsorption ref [31], ref [43]. For label-free electrical and electrochemical sensing, the organization, density, and orientation of immobilized receptors are especially important because the signal depends directly on local interfacial perturbations caused by target binding rather than on secondary labels ref [22].

Beyond natural bioreceptors, synthetic recognition layers are increasingly relevant for robust cancer biosensing. Molecularly imprinted polymers offer chemically stable, low-cost binding sites that can tolerate harsher conditions than proteins and are attractive for biomarkers where antibody storage or batch variability is problematic ref [21]. Taken together, current literature suggests that high-performance cancer biosensors emerge not from the recognition element alone, but from co-optimization of probe identity, immobilization chemistry, antifouling architecture, and nanoscale electrode structure ref [16], ref [31].

subsections.section_title: Biorecognition Elements and Interfacial Engineering for Cancer Biosensors
subsections.subsection_title: Biorecognition Elements and Interfacial Engineering for Cancer Biosensors - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Nucleic-acid-based recognition layers have become central to electrochemical cancer biosensors because sequence programmability enables precise control over affinity, density, and interfacial architecture. DNA probes are particularly attractive for mutation and circulating nucleic-acid analysis, while aptamer-like and DNA nanostructured interfaces can also mediate selective cell capture through multivalent binding. Back-gated graphene field-effect DNA biosensors illustrate how interfacial engineering at atomically thin transducers can translate hybridization events into highly sensitive, label-free electrical readout, provided that probe immobilization and surface cleanliness are carefully managed to preserve carrier transport and reduce nonspecific adsorption ref [22].

Beyond simple probe monolayers, multivalent and hierarchical DNA assemblies improve target capture by increasing local binding avidity and by organizing amplification reactions near the electrode. This concept is especially relevant for rare cancer cell detection, where DNA nanostructured capture interfaces coupled with multibranched hybridization chain reaction can enhance both cell retention and signal generation ref [27]. Similar principles are increasingly applied to extracellular vesicle sensing: exosome biosensors rely on antibodies, aptamers, or nucleic-acid-assisted affinity interfaces, but their performance is strongly dictated by antifouling coatings, nanoscale roughness, and orientation of capture motifs at the transducer surface ref [9].

Interfacial materials further modulate the behavior of biorecognition elements. Carbon nanomaterials offer large electroactive area, facile functionalization, and efficient electron transfer, enabling stable immobilization of DNA, proteins, and vesicle-capture ligands for non-invasive cancer biomarker analysis ref [29]. In enzyme-assisted electrochemical formats, nanomaterial-engineered interfaces can also improve biocatalyst loading, preserve enzymatic activity, and accelerate redox mediation, thereby supporting amplification strategies integrated with affinity recognition ref [37]. These design choices are clinically consequential, as early-stage breast cancer detection platforms show that assay sensitivity depends not only on the biomarker selected, but also on how the recognition element is spatially organized and electronically coupled to the electrode interface ref [38].

subsections.section_title: Biorecognition Elements and Interfacial Engineering for Cancer Biosensors
subsections.subsection_title: Biorecognition Elements and Interfacial Engineering for Cancer Biosensors - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Aptamers and nucleic-acid probes are particularly attractive biorecognition elements for cancer electrochemical biosensors because their sequence programmability enables precise control over affinity, hybridization, and signal transduction at the electrode interface. In cancer biomarker analysis, this is especially important for soluble proteins and microRNAs, where sandwich-type aptamer architectures can improve target selectivity while reducing nonspecific adsorption through steric discrimination and dual-site recognition ref [12]. For nucleic-acid targets, probe density, orientation, and hybridization accessibility at the interface strongly affect sensitivity, making surface engineering inseparable from recognition design ref [16], ref [16].

For microRNA sensing, interfacial engineering typically aims to maximize capture efficiency for short, low-abundance sequences while preserving electron-transfer pathways. DNA-modified electrodes are therefore often combined with catalytic or nanostructured layers that enlarge effective surface area, facilitate probe immobilization, and support amplification chemistries. A representative example is miR-21 detection on a microfluidic paper-based electrochemical/visual platform using spherical cerium dioxide, where the interfacial catalyst contributes to enhanced analytical response under miniaturized conditions ref [31]. More broadly, reviews of microRNA electrochemical biosensors emphasize that antifouling coatings, controlled probe spacing, and hybridization-friendly microenvironments are central to reliable analysis in clinically relevant matrices ref [16].

Beyond antibodies and oligonucleotides, peptides offer a compact recognition format with tunable sequence motifs, good synthetic reproducibility, and straightforward integration into electroactive surfaces. Their shorter dimensions can place binding events closer to the transducer, which is beneficial for impedance and voltammetric readout, although their performance remains highly dependent on immobilization chemistry and conformational freedom at the interface ref [28]. General biomolecular surveys further show that selecting among aptamers, peptides, enzymes, and immunoreagents should be guided by target class, regeneration needs, and matrix complexity, since interfacial stability and bioactivity retention ultimately determine clinical utility more than affinity alone ref [29], ref [16].

subsections.section_title: Biorecognition Elements and Interfacial Engineering for Cancer Biosensors
subsections.subsection_title: Biorecognition Elements and Interfacial Engineering for Cancer Biosensors - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A critical aspect of interfacial engineering in cancer biosensors is the design of transducer surfaces that preserve biorecognition activity while enabling efficient charge transfer. In affinity biosensors, this requires controlling probe density, orientation, antifouling behavior, and nanoscale architecture, since these parameters directly determine target accessibility and impedance or capacitive response ref [17], ref [35]. Nanoporous anodic alumina is illustrative in this regard: its ordered pore structure offers high surface area and tunable confinement, improving immobilization efficiency and signal reproducibility for clinically relevant biomarker detection ref [20].

For nucleic-acid recognition, the electrode interface must support stable probe grafting and discriminate subtle hybridization-induced changes. Comparative impedimetric studies on glassy carbon modified with PANHS, reduced graphene oxide, and MWCNTs show that linker chemistry and nanomaterial selection jointly shape electron-transfer resistance and hybridization sensitivity ref [24]. Likewise, reactive carbon nano-onion surfaces provide defect-rich, electroactive platforms that enhance DNA loading and facilitate sensitive detection of HPV oncogene sequences, underscoring how carbon nanoarchitecture can amplify recognition events without sacrificing specificity ref [23]. Broader analyses of DNA-based electrochemical cancer biosensors similarly emphasize that probe immobilization strategy, spacer design, and hybrid conductive scaffolds are decisive for low-abundance nucleic-acid targets ref [40].

Analogous principles apply to immunosensors for protein biomarkers. Hybrid interfaces such as hydroxyl pillar[5]arene@AuNPs@g-C3N4 combine supramolecular host functionality, metallic conductivity, and large active area to improve antibody loading and PSA recognition performance ref [19]. Chitosan/conductive carbon black coatings on disposable ITO electrodes offer a complementary route, where biopolymer film formation and conductive filler dispersion support stable p53 antibody immobilization and practical assay fabrication ref [13]. Taken together, these studies show that interfacial engineering is not merely auxiliary to biorecognition; it is a co-determinant of selectivity, sensitivity, and operational robustness in electrochemical cancer biosensors ref [17], ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Biorecognition Elements and Interfacial Engineering for Cancer Biosensors
subsections.subsection_title: Biorecognition Elements and Interfacial Engineering for Cancer Biosensors - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A final design dimension in cancer-oriented electrochemical biosensors is the coupling between the recognition element and the interfacial architecture. Immobilization chemistry must preserve the native accessibility and specificity of the probe, since excessive surface crowding, unfavorable orientation, or reactive crosslinking can degrade target binding even when the transducer itself is highly conductive. This principle has been illustrated clearly in enzyme electrodes, where immobilization strategy directly affected retained specificity, underscoring that interfacial engineering is not a passive support step but a determinant of analytical fidelity ref [26].

For nucleic-acid biosensors, control of probe packing density and hybridization environment governs both sensitivity and background current. Label-free electrochemical DNA platforms for breast-cancer gene analysis demonstrate how surface-confined oligonucleotides can transduce sequence recognition without labels, while broader analyses of DNA biosensor detection limits indicate that interface quality, not only electrode material, has been central to progressive performance gains ref [13], ref [37]. Similar effects are seen in aptamer systems: comparative work on two lysozyme aptamers showed that probe sequence and folding behavior translate into different analytical responses on the same platform, highlighting the need to match aptamer structure with the chosen surface chemistry ref [15].

Spacer engineering provides an additional lever for optimizing interfacial recognition. In peptide-based electrochemical biosensors, spacer length was shown to modulate steric accessibility and signal generation for protease targets, a concept directly relevant to cancer biomarker assays involving proteases or cleavage-responsive formats ref [32]. More complex multifunctional interfaces, such as bifunctional nanobiosensors developed for chemokine ligand detection in colorectal cancer cells, further illustrate how co-integrating capture chemistry with nanostructured transduction layers can improve target recruitment and electrochemical readout ref [24]. Collectively, these studies suggest that future cancer biosensors will benefit from treating bioreceptor selection, linker design, and interfacial nanoengineering as a single co-optimized system rather than independent steps ref [26], ref [15], ref [24], ref [32].

subsections.section_title: Nanomaterials and Advanced Electrode Architectures for Signal Enhancement
subsections.subsection_title: Nanomaterials and Advanced Electrode Architectures for Signal Enhancement - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Nanomaterials are central to signal enhancement in electrochemical cancer biosensors because they simultaneously increase electroactive surface area, accelerate interfacial electron transfer, and provide dense anchoring sites for antibodies, aptamers, or nucleic-acid probes. Reviews of nanostructured electrochemical sensing platforms consistently show that metallic nanoparticles, carbon nanostructures, quantum dots, and hybrid composites improve current response and lower detection limits by coupling conductivity with high surface-to-volume ratio ref [54], ref [12]. In cancer biomarker analysis, these effects are especially important for low-abundance targets, where small gains in charge-transfer efficiency or probe loading can markedly improve assay sensitivity ref [16].

A first design axis is the use of engineered electrode coatings and three-dimensional nanoarchitectures. Nanostructured films, porous layers, and composite interfaces create more accessible binding domains while shortening diffusion pathways for redox mediators, which is advantageous in immunosensors and affinity-based devices ref [14], ref [12]. Carbon-based nanostructures and metal–carbon hybrids are widely emphasized as effective transducers because they combine mechanical stability with fast electron transport, enabling more reproducible and amplified faradaic signals ref [54]. Such architectures are also compatible with miniaturized and lab-on-a-chip formats, where high local signal density is needed despite limited geometric electrode area ref [12].

Magnetic nanomaterials add a complementary enhancement strategy by enabling target preconcentration, magnetic separation, and controllable assembly of biorecognition complexes at the electrode surface. This reduces matrix interference and can raise effective analyte concentration before electrochemical readout, an attractive feature for complex cancer samples ref [15], ref [16]. Related nanotechnology-enabled no-wash formats further exploit nanomaterial-mediated capture and signal generation to simplify workflows while retaining high analytical performance, pointing toward practical point-of-care cancer diagnostics based on advanced electrode architectures rather than chemistry alone ref [43].

subsections.section_title: Nanomaterials and Advanced Electrode Architectures for Signal Enhancement
subsections.subsection_title: Nanomaterials and Advanced Electrode Architectures for Signal Enhancement - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Beyond material composition alone, signal enhancement increasingly depends on how nanomaterials are organized into manufacturable electrode architectures. Paper-based electrochemical platforms illustrate this well: porous cellulose networks can host metal, carbon, or oxide nanostructures that enlarge the electroactive area, accelerate capillary-driven mass transport, and support higher bioreceptor loading while preserving low-cost, disposable analysis formats relevant to cancer screening ref [7], ref [38]. Such architecture-level gains are especially important when biomarkers are present at ultralow concentrations in minimally processed samples.

Additive manufacturing further expands the design space by enabling three-dimensional electrodes, integrated fluidic features, and reproducible deposition of conductive composites. Reviews of 3D-printed sensors and biosensors show that printed architectures can tune roughness, porosity, and current distribution, thereby improving electron-transfer efficiency and facilitating multiplexed assay integration ref [36]. Related work on nanomaterials, magnetic beads, and microfluidic systems likewise emphasizes that combining engineered electrode geometries with sample-handling modules can shorten diffusion paths and enhance capture efficiency, which is highly attractive for compact cancer-diagnostic devices ref [17].

At the nanoelectronic end of the spectrum, graphene field-effect transistor architectures demonstrate how atomically thin transducers convert interfacial binding into highly sensitive, label-free electrical readout, with scalable fabrication being a key advantage for translational biosensing ref [22]. Carbon nanomaterials more broadly remain central because graphene, nanotubes, and related allotropes provide high conductivity, large surface area, and favorable immobilization interfaces for nucleic-acid and protein biomarkers ref [29]. In enzyme-assisted electrochemical schemes, nanostructured supports can also improve enzyme loading, orientational stability, and electrocatalytic turnover, reinforcing the broader principle that advanced electrode architecture and nanomaterial function must be co-optimized rather than treated separately ref [37].

subsections.section_title: Nanomaterials and Advanced Electrode Architectures for Signal Enhancement
subsections.subsection_title: Nanomaterials and Advanced Electrode Architectures for Signal Enhancement - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A major route to signal enhancement in electrochemical cancer biosensors is the use of catalytic and conductive nanocomposites that couple high surface area with accelerated interfacial charge transfer. Carbon nanotubes are particularly valuable in this context because their one-dimensional conductive pathways improve electron transport while also increasing the density of immobilized probes on miniaturized electrodes, features that are highly compatible with point-of-care cancer testing formats ref [25]. Similar benefits are observed with intrinsically conducting polymer composites, where the polymer matrix provides mechanical integrity and facile biofunctionalization, while embedded nanophases increase conductivity, electrocatalytic activity, and stability of the sensing layer ref [32].

Metallic and hybrid nanoarchitectures further amplify current responses by introducing electrocatalytic hot spots and lowering overpotentials. Bimetallic Pd-Au clusters exemplify how compositionally engineered nanostructures can outperform monometallic surfaces through synergistic catalytic effects and rapid electron-transfer kinetics, a principle readily transferable from metabolite sensing to redox-assisted cancer biomarker assays ref [62]. More broadly, nanomaterial design strategies developed in cholesterol and other enzymatic biosensors highlight the importance of tailoring morphology, porosity, and surface chemistry to preserve biomolecule activity while maximizing catalytic accessibility at the electrode interface ref [19], ref [61].

Advanced electrode architectures increasingly combine these material advantages with robust immobilization chemistry. For example, diazonium-functionalized boron-doped diamond modified with a multi-walled carbon nanotube-tyrosinase hybrid film demonstrates how a chemically stable substrate, covalent grafting layer, and conductive nanotube-enzyme coating can jointly improve sensitivity and operational durability ref [39]. In parallel, catalyst-integrated paper and microfluidic platforms using spherical CeO2 show that nanostructured catalytic interfaces can deliver strong signal gain even in low-volume, portable nucleic-acid assays such as miR-21 detection, underscoring the relevance of hierarchical material-electrode integration for practical cancer diagnostics ref [31].

subsections.section_title: Nanomaterials and Advanced Electrode Architectures for Signal Enhancement
subsections.subsection_title: Nanomaterials and Advanced Electrode Architectures for Signal Enhancement - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A major strategy for signal enhancement is the deliberate engineering of nano-enabled electrode interfaces that simultaneously increase electroactive area, accelerate charge transport, and provide dense anchoring sites for bioreceptors. Graphene-derived platforms are especially valuable in this regard because their high carrier mobility and large accessible surface support low-noise transduction and efficient coupling of affinity events to electrical output ref [17]. More broadly, nanomaterial-based amperometric biosensors exploit metallic nanoparticles, carbon nanostructures, and hybrid composites to amplify faradaic currents through improved electron-transfer kinetics and catalytic activity ref [19].

Representative cancer-biomarker platforms illustrate how these principles are translated into practical electrode designs. A hydroxyl pillar[5]arene@AuNPs@g-C3N4 hybrid was used to construct an ultrasensitive PSA immunosensor, where supramolecular host functionality, gold nanoparticles, and graphitic carbon nitride jointly enhanced antibody immobilization and interfacial conductivity ref [18]. Likewise, a chitosan/conductive carbon black composite on disposable ITO electrodes provided a biocompatible yet conductive matrix for p53 detection, highlighting the value of low-cost composite coatings for increasing loading capacity while preserving electrochemical responsiveness ref [13].

Beyond these examples, advanced architectures based on nanoporous templates and alternative carbon nanostructures further broaden design options for cancer biosensing. Nanoporous anodic alumina offers ordered, high-surface-area confinement that can improve probe organization and mass transport, which is advantageous for clinically relevant biomarker assays ref [20]. Carbon nano-onion modified glassy carbon electrodes have shown enhanced sensitivity for HPV oncogene DNA sensing, and comparative impedimetric studies on RGO- and MWCNT-modified glassy carbon electrodes confirm that nanostructure selection strongly influences hybridization efficiency and interfacial resistance changes ref [23], ref [24]. Even outside oncology, nickel nanoparticle-modified electrodes demonstrate how catalytic nanometals can drive ultratrace electrochemical detection, reinforcing a transferable design principle for highly sensitive cancer biomarker platforms ref [21].

subsections.section_title: Nanomaterials and Advanced Electrode Architectures for Signal Enhancement
subsections.subsection_title: Nanomaterials and Advanced Electrode Architectures for Signal Enhancement - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Hybrid nanoarchitectures that integrate conductive carbons, catalytic metals, and semiconductor scaffolds are increasingly important for signal enhancement because they simultaneously improve charge transport, enlarge the effective surface area, and provide robust anchoring sites for biorecognition layers. For example, graphitized carbon nanofiber–Pt nanoparticle composites and Au nanoparticle-decorated reduced graphene oxide illustrate how hierarchical conductive networks can accelerate interfacial electron transfer while amplifying faradaic responses, design principles that are directly transferable to cancer biomarker biosensors requiring low detection limits and rapid response times ref [12], ref [33].

A complementary strategy is to tailor the nanomaterial chemistry to support biomolecule immobilization and redox mediation. Covalently functionalized single-walled carbon nanotubes with polytyrosine offer abundant functional groups and improved electrocatalytic behavior for NADH-related transduction, whereas Au nanoparticle-encapsulated tubular TiO2 nanoclusters provide a high-area, biocompatible scaffold for thiolated biomolecules, combining the affinity of gold chemistry with the structural stability of oxide supports ref [18], ref [27]. Nitrogen-doped graphene quantum dots add another useful dimension by contributing high conductivity, edge-site activity, and facile surface functionalization, making them attractive as signal-promoting interlayers in electrochemical biosensing platforms ref [22].

Although several of these studies were demonstrated in non-cancer analytical settings, their architectural lessons are highly relevant to oncology-oriented devices. Nanostructured DNA electrodes have already been used to probe drug-induced interactions with DNA from cancer cells, highlighting the value of nanoscale interfaces for enhancing sensitivity to subtle nucleic-acid events ref [39]. Likewise, a bifunctional nanobiosensor developed for chemokine ligand analysis in a colorectal cancer cell line underscores how multifunctional nanoplatforms can support both recognition and signal generation within a single electrode design ref [24]. Overall, advanced electrode engineering is shifting from single-material modification toward multifunctional, synergistic nanocomposites that better satisfy the sensitivity, selectivity, and stability requirements of electrochemical cancer biomarker analysis ref [22], ref [24], ref [33].

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Biosensor Applications in Cancer Biomarker Detection
subsections.subsection_title: Electrochemical Biosensor Applications in Cancer Biomarker Detection - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Protein biomarkers remain the most established clinical targets for electrochemical cancer biosensors, making immunosensor-oriented applications a logical starting point for this section. In these systems, antibodies or antibody-derived recognition elements are immobilized on conductive interfaces to capture tumor-associated proteins such as PSA, CEA, CA markers, or p53, while electrochemical transduction converts binding events into current, potential, impedance, or capacitance changes. This application space has been shaped by the broader maturation of electrochemical immunosensors and antibody-based analytical platforms, which provide the conceptual basis for selective protein analysis in complex biological samples ref [14], ref [32].

Reported strategies for cancer protein detection increasingly rely on nanostructured electrodes to improve loading of capture probes, accelerate electron transfer, and amplify analytical signals. Reviews of nanomaterial-enabled electrochemical sensors describe how metal nanoparticles, carbon nanostructures, and hybrid nanocomposites support lower detection limits and wider dynamic ranges, while related lab-on-a-chip integrations favor miniaturization and multiplexing for translational diagnostics ref [54], ref [12]. For cancer applications specifically, these design principles have enabled sensitive biosensing in serum and other clinically relevant matrices, often with simplified assay workflows and reduced reagent consumption ref [16], ref [43].

From an analytical perspective, label-free electrical and electrochemical formats are especially attractive for protein biomarkers because they can directly probe interfacial changes after antigen binding and thus reduce assay complexity. Their clinical value, however, depends not only on nominal sensitivity but also on figures of merit such as selectivity, reproducibility, linear range, limit of detection, and robustness in real samples. These performance criteria are repeatedly emphasized in discussions of label-free protein biosensing and in broader evaluations of biosensors for clinical use, underscoring that diagnostic applicability requires rigorous analytical validation in addition to materials innovation ref [22], ref [37].

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Biosensor Applications in Cancer Biomarker Detection
subsections.subsection_title: Electrochemical Biosensor Applications in Cancer Biomarker Detection - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A rapidly expanding application area for electrochemical biosensors is the detection of extracellular vesicles and intact tumor cells, which complement soluble protein and nucleic-acid biomarkers by preserving phenotypic information from the tumor microenvironment. Exosome-oriented platforms are particularly attractive because cancer-derived vesicles carry surface proteins, nucleic acids, and lipids that can be sampled from minimally invasive liquid biopsies, enabling early diagnosis and disease monitoring; recent reviews emphasize electrochemical transduction as a practical route for sensitive and potentially point-of-care exosome analysis ref [9].

At the cellular level, electrochemical strategies increasingly exploit multivalent recognition and nucleic-acid amplification to improve the capture of rare malignant cells. DNA nanostructured biosensors combined with multibranched hybridization chain reaction amplification illustrate this trend, offering enhanced binding avidity and amplified electrochemical readout for cancer-cell detection, thereby addressing the low abundance and heterogeneity that often limit circulating tumor cell assays ref [27]. Such designs show how biosensor architecture can be tuned not only for signal gain but also for selective interrogation of whole-cell biomarkers.

Materials engineering remains central to these applications. Carbon nanomaterial-based interfaces have been widely used to improve electron transfer, increase effective surface area, and support antibody-, aptamer-, or nucleic-acid-mediated recognition in non-invasive cancer biomarker testing, including vesicular and cellular targets ref [29]. Although not cancer-specific, real-time electrochemical detection of interleukin-6 with needle-shaped microelectrodes also demonstrates how miniaturized formats can support dynamic monitoring of clinically relevant inflammatory markers that are increasingly studied in oncology contexts ref [14]. In parallel, early breast-cancer screening studies underscore the broader diagnostic value of integrating electrochemical biomarker panels with accessible sampling strategies to improve sensitivity at preclinical stages ref [38].

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Biosensor Applications in Cancer Biomarker Detection
subsections.subsection_title: Electrochemical Biosensor Applications in Cancer Biomarker Detection - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A major application area of electrochemical biosensors in cancer diagnosis is nucleic-acid biomarker analysis, especially circulating microRNAs (miRNAs), whose abnormal expression is closely associated with tumor initiation, progression, and metastasis. Electrochemical platforms are well suited to miRNA sensing because they combine low sample consumption, high sensitivity, and compatibility with miniaturized readout formats. Reviews of electrochemical miRNA biosensing emphasize that hybridization-based recognition, signal amplification by nanomaterials or enzymes, and disposable electrode formats have made these systems increasingly attractive for clinically relevant cancer assays ref [39], ref [16].

Within this class, sandwich-type and label-free designs represent two important analytical routes. Aptamer- or nucleic-acid-assisted sandwich architectures improve selectivity by using dual recognition events and can be adapted to low-abundance cancer targets, while label-free electrochemical transduction reduces assay complexity and supports rapid testing in minimally processed samples ref [12], ref [14]. These strategies are particularly valuable for short miRNA sequences, where discrimination of closely related family members is essential for avoiding false-positive cancer assignments ref [39].

Recent application trends also show strong convergence between electrochemical miRNA sensing and portable multiplexed platforms. Microfluidic chip-integrated electronic biosensors enable parallel analysis, reduced reagent volumes, and improved automation, which are important for multi-marker cancer panels rather than single-analyte testing ref [24]. A representative example is the microfluidic paper-based electrochemical/visual biosensor developed for miR-21, a widely studied oncogenic miRNA, illustrating how catalyst-assisted signal generation can support ultrasensitive and potentially point-of-care cancer screening workflows ref [31]. Although similar integration concepts are also discussed in biosensor reviews beyond oncology, including neurodegenerative biomarker detection, the same principles of multiplexing, portability, and low-cost electroanalysis are directly relevant to translational cancer diagnostics ref [23].

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Biosensor Applications in Cancer Biomarker Detection
subsections.subsection_title: Electrochemical Biosensor Applications in Cancer Biomarker Detection - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Nucleic-acid and mutation-oriented biomarkers form a distinct application space for electrochemical biosensors because they enable direct interrogation of oncogenic sequences, viral genes, and tumor-suppressor alterations. Recent analytical progress has emphasized DNA-based electrochemical platforms for cancer biomarkers, including hybridization sensors and sequence-specific assays that translate target recognition into current, impedance, or capacitance changes, often with substantial gains in sensitivity from nanostructured interfaces and signal amplification chemistries ref [40].

Representative examples illustrate how these strategies are adapted to clinically relevant cancer targets. Reactive carbon nano-onion modified glassy carbon electrodes have been used for sensitive detection of human papillomavirus oncogene sequences, demonstrating the utility of conductive carbon nanostructures for cervical-cancer-related nucleic acid analysis ref [23]. Likewise, impedimetric DNA hybridization on modified glassy carbon electrodes incorporating PANHS, reduced graphene oxide, and multiwalled carbon nanotubes highlights how surface chemistry and electron-transfer mediation govern hybridization efficiency and label-free readout quality ref [24]. Beyond individual transducers, nanoporous anodic alumina-based biosensor architectures have been reviewed as versatile platforms for clinically significant biomarkers, including nucleic-acid targets, owing to their high surface area, controllable pore geometry, and favorable immobilization characteristics ref [20].

This nucleic-acid-centered application space also connects to broader tumor biology through protein and gene-network markers. For example, electrochemical immunosensing of p53 has been demonstrated on disposable ITO electrodes modified with chitosan/conductive carbon black composites, showing how tumor-suppressor pathway assessment can be integrated into electrochemical formats ref [13]. In parallel, ultrasensitive PSA immunosensing with hydroxyl pillar[5]arene@AuNPs@g-C3N4 hybrid materials exemplifies the complementary role of protein biomarkers in prostate cancer diagnostics ref [19]. Taken together, these studies suggest that future clinically useful systems will likely combine DNA, viral, and protein markers in multiplex electrochemical formats to improve cancer specificity and staging capability ref [40].

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Biosensor Applications in Cancer Biomarker Detection
subsections.subsection_title: Electrochemical Biosensor Applications in Cancer Biomarker Detection - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A further application area concerns nucleic-acid-associated and extracellular-vesicle biomarkers, which are increasingly important because they capture tumor genotype and intercellular signaling with high disease specificity. Electrochemical biosensors are particularly well suited to this class through direct hybridization readout, label-free impedance or voltammetric transduction, and nanostructure-enabled signal amplification, enabling sensitive analysis of oncogene sequences and exosome-associated cargos in clinically relevant matrices ref [25], ref [37].

Representative studies illustrate how these strategies have been translated to cancer-relevant targets. Label-free electrochemical DNA biosensors have been reported for breast-cancer gene marker detection, demonstrating the practicality of sequence-selective interfaces without secondary labels ref [13]. Nanostructured DNA sensing platforms have also been used to interrogate drug–DNA interactions in cancer-cell-derived DNA, showing that electrochemical readout can extend beyond simple presence/absence testing to functional analysis of therapeutic effects ref [39]. From a broader analytical perspective, longitudinal evaluation of electrochemical DNA biosensors indicates sustained improvement in detection limits, supporting their suitability for low-abundance circulating nucleic acid biomarkers ref [37].

This application space also overlaps with soluble signaling mediators and disease-specific liquid-biopsy markers. A bifunctional nanobiosensor for chemokine ligand detection in colorectal cancer cells highlights the relevance of electrochemical platforms for monitoring tumor-associated inflammatory communication ref [24]. In parallel, exosome-oriented biosensor developments point toward minimally invasive profiling of vesicle cargo and surface signatures, while melanoma diagnostics literature underscores the continuing need for rapid, sensitive adjunct tools capable of complementing conventional analytical workflows ref [25], ref [34]. Collectively, these reports suggest that electrochemical biosensors are evolving toward integrated assessment of circulating DNA, exosomes, and related molecular signals for earlier and more informative cancer detection ref [25], ref [13], ref [24].

subsections.section_title: Device Integration, Translational Challenges, and Future Perspectives
subsections.subsection_title: Device Integration, Translational Challenges, and Future Perspectives - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A central step in translating electrochemical cancer biomarker assays from benchtop demonstrations to practical diagnostics is device-level integration of sensing interfaces with fluid handling, sample preparation, and readout electronics. Microfluidic integration is especially important because it reduces reagent consumption, shortens diffusion distances, and enables controlled transport, multiplexing, and automation within lab-on-a-chip formats, all of which are highly relevant for low-volume clinical specimens such as serum, plasma, and whole blood ref [13]. In parallel, functional nanomaterials and nanostructures have been used not only to improve electrode sensitivity, but also to support miniaturized architectures compatible with integrated electrochemical and lab-on-a-chip platforms ref [12].

For cancer biomarker detection, however, integration must preserve analytical performance under realistic biological conditions. Reviews of cancer biosensor development emphasize that many high-performing prototypes are still validated mainly in buffered media rather than complex matrices, creating a gap between proof-of-concept sensitivity and clinical robustness ref [16]. This challenge is consistent with broader analyses of clinical sensor figures of merit, which show that limit of detection alone is insufficient; selectivity, reproducibility, calibration stability, dynamic range, and uncertainty in patient samples are equally decisive for translational value ref [37]. Likewise, strategies developed in enzyme biosensors to safeguard operation in biological fluids—such as antifouling interfaces, controlled immobilization, and mitigation of matrix effects—are directly relevant to integrated electrochemical cancer biosensors ref [17].

An important future direction is therefore the development of fully integrated, low-step or no-wash systems that couple nanostructured electrochemical transducers with automated fluidics and simplified assay workflows. No-wash biosensing concepts are particularly attractive for in vitro cancer diagnostics because they reduce operator dependence and are more compatible with point-of-care deployment than multistep laboratory protocols ref [43]. Overall, successful device integration will depend less on maximizing signal amplification in isolation and more on co-optimizing materials, microfluidic architecture, assay simplicity, and clinically meaningful analytical validation ref [12], ref [13], ref [37].

subsections.section_title: Device Integration, Translational Challenges, and Future Perspectives
subsections.subsection_title: Device Integration, Translational Challenges, and Future Perspectives - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central translational step for electrochemical cancer biosensors is the integration of the sensing interface with low-cost sample handling, signal readout, and user-facing hardware. Paper-based platforms are especially attractive because they combine capillary-driven fluid transport, disposability, and compatibility with nanomaterial-enabled signal amplification, making them suitable for decentralized screening workflows ref [58]. Microfluidic integration further improves control over reagent delivery, washing, and multiplexing, which is important for handling complex clinical matrices and reducing operator dependence at the point of care ref [12], ref [17]. In parallel, 3D printing offers a route to rapid prototyping of housings, fluidic manifolds, and even sensing components, thereby shortening the design-build-test cycle and supporting application-specific device customization ref [48].

Readout architecture is equally critical for practical deployment. Smartphone-assisted platforms can convert miniaturized assays into portable diagnostic systems by coupling electrochemical or colorimetric outputs to image analysis, cloud connectivity, and simplified user interfaces; this broader trend is reinforced by both smartphone biosensor reviews and integrated paper-based demonstrations ref [11], ref [36]. However, as devices become more compact, front-end electronics and current acquisition circuitry increasingly define achievable detection limits. In this context, CMOS current-interface noise, drift, and dynamic-range constraints become nontrivial engineering bottlenecks, particularly for low-abundance biomarker measurement where electrochemical currents are small and susceptible to interference ref [25].

Beyond laboratory proof-of-concept, manufacturable integration demands reproducible fabrication across sensor, package, and electronics. The scalable production of graphene FET biosensors illustrates how wafer-level processes can improve uniformity and throughput, although such approaches must still be reconciled with biorecognition immobilization stability and clinical calibration requirements ref [22]. Overall, future electrochemical cancer biosensors will likely converge toward hybrid formats that combine paper or microfluidic cartridges, smartphone-linked analytics, and manufacturable electronic readout modules, with design decisions driven as much by systems engineering as by analytical sensitivity alone ref [58], ref [12], ref [25].

subsections.section_title: Device Integration, Translational Challenges, and Future Perspectives
subsections.subsection_title: Device Integration, Translational Challenges, and Future Perspectives - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central translational requirement for electrochemical cancer biosensors is the integration of sensing chemistry with low-cost fluid handling and user-friendly readout. Paper-based electrochemical platforms are especially attractive because they combine capillary-driven transport, inexpensive substrates, and compatibility with disposable testing formats, while microfluidic paper architectures can support sample pretreatment and multi-step assays in a compact footprint ref [78]. Representative microfluidic paper electrochemical/visual systems for miRNA analysis further illustrate how integrated layouts can merge amplification, catalysis, and dual-mode output, which is highly relevant for decentralized cancer screening ref [31].

Beyond simple strip tests, chip-level microfluidic integration enables multiplexing, controlled reagent delivery, and reduced sample consumption, all of which are important for panels of protein, nucleic-acid, or ionic biomarkers rather than single-analyte measurements ref [24]. In this context, ion-selective membrane microfluidics provides an additional design space for regulating transport, preconcentration, and local chemical environments, offering routes to improve analytical robustness in complex biofluids ref [21]. Carbon-nanotube-enabled point-of-care devices also remain important because they can couple high interfacial sensitivity with portable transduction hardware, although reproducibility and standardized fabrication still limit broad clinical deployment ref [25].

Future device integration will likely depend not only on miniaturization but also on metrological rigor and digital connectivity. For label-free formats in particular, realistic estimation of uncertainty and limit of detection is essential, since apparent gains in sensitivity may not translate into dependable clinical decision thresholds without standardized analytical validation ref [16]. More generally, diagnostic label-free biosensors must balance simplicity against fouling, drift, and matrix effects in real samples ref [14]. Smartphone-linked readers may help address this gap by enabling portable potentiostatic control, cloud-assisted analysis, and longitudinal data capture, although the analytical workflow must be tightly standardized for medical use ref [38].

subsections.section_title: Device Integration, Translational Challenges, and Future Perspectives
subsections.subsection_title: Device Integration, Translational Challenges, and Future Perspectives - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A central translational challenge is converting high-performance electrochemical assays into integrated, easy-to-operate platforms that preserve analytical fidelity outside controlled laboratory settings. Biosensors-on-chip offer a route to combine sample handling, transduction, and signal processing in compact formats, but system-level integration often exposes new constraints related to fluid routing, electrode reproducibility, packaging, and electrical interfacing that are less visible in benchtop demonstrations ref [22]. Similar concerns apply to affinity-based formats more broadly, where surface functionalization stability, nonspecific adsorption, and limited shelf life can undermine clinical robustness despite excellent proof-of-concept sensitivity ref [17].

From a manufacturing perspective, platform choice strongly influences scalability and use-case suitability. Paper-based chemiresistive and related low-cost architectures are attractive for decentralized cancer screening because they reduce fabrication complexity and enable disposable operation, yet they still require tighter control of substrate variability, environmental sensitivity, and calibration transfer across production lots ref [42]. In parallel, nanoporous anodic alumina provides a more structured route to high-surface-area sensing interfaces with favorable tunability and multiplexing potential, but translation depends on reproducible nanostructure fabrication and seamless integration with fluidic and electronic modules ref [20]. For label-free electrochemical readout, impedimetric and redox-capacitive schemes are particularly promising because they simplify assay workflows; however, they are also highly sensitive to interfacial drift, parasitic capacitances, and matrix-dependent artifacts, which complicates operation in real clinical specimens ref [35].

Looking forward, clinically deployable cancer biosensors will likely emerge from co-design across biorecognition chemistry, chip architecture, and manufacturable electronics rather than from sensitivity optimization alone. DNA-based electrochemical biosensing illustrates this point well: although nucleic-acid assays can achieve excellent selectivity and multiplexing potential, practical implementation requires streamlined immobilization, standardized hybridization conditions, and validated workflows for complex samples ref [40]. More generally, future affinity biosensors must prioritize robustness, automation, and regulatory-compatible quality control, including batch-to-batch consistency and long-term stability, if they are to progress from promising prototypes to routine oncology diagnostics ref [17], ref [22].

subsections.section_title: Device Integration, Translational Challenges, and Future Perspectives
subsections.subsection_title: Device Integration, Translational Challenges, and Future Perspectives - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Looking forward, the most credible route to clinical impact lies in convergent platforms that combine electrochemical transduction with simplified sampling, miniaturized fluid handling, and decentralized readout. Recent work on nucleic-acid and exosome biosensors indicates that future cancer diagnostics will increasingly rely on multimodal liquid-biopsy targets rather than single-analyte assays, demanding integrated devices capable of handling low-abundance, heterogeneous biomarkers in complex matrices ref [25]. Capillary-driven formats are particularly attractive in this context because they reduce external instrumentation and user steps; the Pt@AuNPs-integrated quantitative capillary biosensor exemplifies how nanostructured electrochemical interfaces can be embedded into portable point-of-care architectures without abandoning quantitative performance ref [36].

A major translational challenge, however, is that gains in analytical sensitivity do not automatically translate into clinical usefulness. Historical analyses of electrochemical DNA biosensors show a persistent trend toward ever-lower detection limits, but these improvements must be balanced against reproducibility, calibration stability, and matrix tolerance under real operating conditions ref [37]. This is especially relevant for label-free gene assays, such as breast-cancer-marker DNA sensors, where surface chemistry, nonspecific adsorption, and batch-to-batch electrode variability can dominate performance outside controlled laboratory settings ref [13]. Similarly, bifunctional nanobiosensors developed for colorectal-cancer-associated chemokine detection illustrate the promise of multiplexed or dual-function formats, while also underscoring the need for standardized validation workflows and clinically meaningful cutoff values ref [24].

Future perspectives therefore extend beyond sensor optimization toward evidence-based clinical integration. Disease-specific diagnostic pathways, including those discussed for melanoma, make clear that electrochemical biosensors will be adopted only if they complement existing diagnostic algorithms, shorten turnaround time, or improve access in resource-limited settings ref [34]. In practice, the next generation of cancer biosensors should prioritize manufacturable disposable formats, interoperable readers, prospective clinical studies, and panels that jointly measure nucleic acids, vesicles, and protein markers to improve robustness across patient populations ref [25], ref [36], ref [34].
